column4: Great famine. Cultivators fled to Malwa for food. Government called them back and made remissions of rent, and also made advances in the shape of Tuccavee. During this year of great distress the then Government distributed grain free of charge; some portions of the Purgunnahs were not-withstanding desolated. The information is obtained from the old hereditary revenue officers. No record, private or public, is forthcoming.
Years of dearness, but not of famine. The scarcity was caused by the plunderings of the Pindarees.
Great famine, and much distress; but no detail information is procurable.

Great famine. People fled for grain to other countries. Some of the people offered their services for food, while others lived by begging; some of them took refuge at Surat, where the Native Shaookars, and particularly the Dutch Merchants, supplied the people with rice free of charge, or by receiving a reasonable price, according as the people were indigent or otherwise. The then Nawab of Surat also helped the distressed poor to a considerable degree, and made arrangements by which the grain dealers were made to sell according to a certain nerrick a fixed quantity of grain to each individual.

This was a year of great famine, and scarcity of water and food to men and animals. The then Government procured grain, opened grain shops, and supplied each family with the requisite quantity of grain as far as possible, but the supply not being sufficient, large numbers of men and animals began to die; so the people with their cattle fled to Malwa, where several of them died, and others returned on the return of the monsoon.

Grain scarce, but not so scarce as to produce great hardship. The cultivators were allowed remission by Government, and advances were also made to them in the shape of Tuccavee; so they had not much difficulty in returning to their former state.
Rain was scanty, but not so scanty as to cause great distress from want of water and grain, so the people had not to leave their native land.

There was an insufficient fall of rain in general. In some eight or ten seacoast villages there was a complete failure of rain; so the people of these villages left their homes and settled themselves in foreign territories, while others who became indigent received the Tuccavee (advances) from Government, and were allowed reasonable remissions in the Jummabundy settlement, in order to enable them to settle themselves and perform their occupations in the then next rainy season.

No great famine has taken place since the accession of the British Government. In Sumvut 1874, A. D. 1818, however, in some years crops were injured owing to the scarcity of rain, or the overflowing of the river. In such times as this Government allowed remissions of rent to the cultivators, and made donations to enable the people to build houses. Government also found work for the people by opening public works, such as sinking and repairing wells, clearing tanks, &c., so the people had not to fly for grain to other provinces. The price of grain and other necessaries of life between the Sumvut 1816 and 1821 was not better than the famine prices in the years preceding the accession of the British power, and, though the prices have declined since the Sumvut 1822, the decrease is only slight.
